{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-pa-c","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"08ab60cf70b07dd70cf2baf82befef24a4ab21a57ac7ef6c7e2cb490b04e46ca","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-pa-class-c:lineage:56","source_registry_sha256":"643bc755bc144bbb64c82e5b21691c27918519b2f96f9b0ff96b63899c04fddb","source_liveness_sha256":"d125293461efac0b369397a252e58fe1686ca24cdc89a306e2ea205c1feddb7c"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Driving emergencies","heading":"C — Driving emergencies","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Driving emergencies

FACT_ID: sec13-F01 | anchor: A01
Hold the steering wheel with both hands, especially when rapid emergency steering may be needed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F02 | anchor: A01
At higher speeds, less steering movement is needed to shift the vehicle sideways. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F03 | anchor: A01
The handbook recommends hands at nine and three or eight and four on the wheel, with thumbs along its face rather than inside the rim. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F04 | anchor: A01
The ten-and-two hand position is described as acceptable but increases airbag-related arm and hand injury risk. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F05 | anchor: A01
Hand-over-hand steering reaches across to grasp the opposite rim and pull across the top repeatedly as needed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F06 | anchor: A01
Push-pull steering alternates one hand pushing upward with the other sliding up and pulling down. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F07 | anchor: A01
Crash-injury protection includes proper belts, adjusted head restraints and sitting at least ten inches from the airbag. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F08 | anchor: A01
Know from the owner's manual whether the vehicle uses conventional brakes or ABS before an emergency occurs. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F09 | anchor: A01
For urgent braking without ABS, repeatedly press and release the pedal rather than slamming hard enough to lock the wheels. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F10 | anchor: A01
For urgent braking with ABS, keep firm continuous pedal pressure and do not pump. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F11 | anchor: A01
Mechanical noise and mild pedal pulses during ABS braking are not reasons to become alarmed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F12 | anchor: A01
On a wet- or ice-road skid, look and steer toward the intended path; turn left if the rear slides left and right if it slides right. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F13 | anchor: A01
Be ready for an opposite skid after a correction and counter it by steering in the new rearward-slide direction. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F14 | anchor: A01
Do not apply the brakes while correcting a skid because wheel lock can remove steering control. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0065]

FACT_ID: sec13-F15 | anchor: A02
Even six inches of floodwater can cause loss of control and float some small vehicles. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F16 | anchor: A02
Twelve inches of moving water can float many cars, and two feet can move most SUVs and pickups. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F17 | anchor: A02
Do not attempt a flooded road; choose another route and never drive through or around a flood closure barrier. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F18 | anchor: A02
Floodwater may conceal missing pavement or bridges and can weaken the roadway; darkness makes the hazard harder to see. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F19 | anchor: A02
If stuck in floodwater, leave the vehicle quickly and move to higher ground. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F20 | anchor: A02
For a stuck accelerator, keep watching the road and try tapping or lifting the pedal with a toe, never reaching down by hand. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F21 | anchor: A02
If the accelerator remains stuck, shift immediately to neutral and brake; the engine may race while wheel power is removed. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F22 | anchor: A02
After slowing safely from a stuck accelerator, steer off the road, stop, turn off the engine and activate hazards. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F23 | anchor: A02
If a stuck accelerator requires an immediate stop, use ignition OFF rather than LOCK, then brake, expecting greater steering and braking effort. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F24 | anchor: A02
A split-system brake warning can leave braking on two of four wheels, probably a front and a rear, while increasing pedal travel, effort and stopping distance. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

FACT_ID: sec13-F25 | anchor: A02
With partial brake failure, use a lower gear to help slow and pull into a safe roadside place or service station. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0066]

Misconceptions: emergency braking differs with ABS; OFF and LOCK ignition positions are not interchangeable; floodwater depth does not guarantee a safe crossing.
Mnemonics: keep control, reduce power, choose a safe path and secure help.
Glossary: ABS is anti-lock braking; a blowout is sudden tire failure; a pavement drop-off leaves wheels below road level.
